title: I understand everything
setting: A first conversation with somebody who studied English at school and stopped.

lines.t: How would you describe your English?
I understand everything, I just can't speak.
Everyone says that sentence. When did you last study?
School. And a course in 2016 that I didn't finish.
So you're a false beginner, which is the easiest kind to teach.
It doesn't feel easy. Everything is rusty.
Rusty comes back fast. Starting from scratch is the slow one, and you're not doing that.
I can get by in a hotel. Not in a meeting.
In a hotel nobody interrupts you. Do you still build the sentence in your mother tongue first?
Every time. By the time it's ready, they're talking about something else.
Then we brush up on what's there and build the meeting on top. What's your language level, honestly?
I'd say B1. My wife would say A2.

title: Correct me every time
setting: Week one and week three of the same request.

lines.t: Correct me every time. I want to hear all of it.
You say that now. Ask me again in three weeks.
I mean it.
I know. Everybody means it in week one.
So what do you actually do?
I correct what stops people understanding you, and I let the rest go until Thursday.
And if I don't understand the correction?
Ask for clarification. "Why is that wrong" is the best question in this room.
Is there homework?
Twenty minutes. Three sentences you actually thought about beat two pages you filled in on the bus.
A colleague offered to be my practice partner.
Take it. A practice partner is worth two lessons, as long as you both stay honest about the mistakes.
And the role play? I'd rather not.
Nobody wants the role play. Everybody remembers it a month later.
Fine. Should I take notes during it?
Afterwards. And revise them on Thursday, because on Thursday they're actually worth something.

title: It arrived in the lift
setting: A student describes the moment a word refused to come.

lines.t: I drew a blank in the meeting today. Completely.
On which word?
One I'd used twice that morning. It was on the tip of my tongue for ten minutes.
And it arrived afterwards, in the lift.
In the lift. How did you know?
It always does. What did you say instead?
I described it. The paper that says the goods arrived.
That's the whole skill. The word rings a bell now, so you'll keep it.
There was another one. I said "eventually" when I meant "possibly".
A false friend, and the one every Bulgarian falls for. The meeting heard a promise.
Should I make flashcards for these? Do I memorise the list?
Make the list, then say each one once in a real sentence. People who memorise lists can recite lists.
And the words I still lose?
Write down the ones you forgot in public. You'll never look it up twice.

title: The day his boss left the room
setting: Why the same person is fluent in one room and silent in another.

lines.t: You were fluent for ten minutes in here. No stopping, no searching.
In here it's easy. In the meeting I'm tongue-tied.
What happens in the first sentence?
I stumble over a word, then I mumble the rest so nobody hears the mistake.
So the mistake is quiet and the silence is loud. Which one costs you more?
The silence. I know that and I still do it.
Everybody hesitates. Native speakers hesitate in a way nobody notices.
Last week I lost my train of thought completely and just stopped.
Say "sorry, let me start again" out loud. It buys you four seconds and sounds deliberate.
Funny thing. The day my boss was away I held a conversation for twenty minutes and thought on my feet the whole time.

title: Ninety per cent of a meeting
setting: Understanding turns out to depend on the room, not the English.

lines.t: My listening is getting worse, not better.
Where? Be specific.
On calls. And in the café on Fridays.
Background noise. That isn't your English, that's the room.
In the office I get the gist of everything.
Getting the gist covers ninety per cent of a meeting and nobody admits it.
The Irish supplier is impossible. His accent defeats me.
Ask him to speak slowly. He will, for two sentences, and that's usually enough.
And four people talk over each other on that call anyway.
Then say so. "Could we take one at a time" is a sentence the English speakers want too.
And when I don't catch something, I pretend I did.
"Sorry, I didn't catch what you said" has never once made anybody look bad. Watch subtitles in English this month and the rest gets easier anyway.

title: Nobody decides to quit
setting: A student returns after a month away and explains himself.

lines.t: Four weeks. What happened?
Nothing dramatic. Work got busy and I fell behind.
That's how it always goes. Nobody decides to quit, they lose momentum.
I kept meaning to come back, and the longer I left it the worse it felt.
The gap is never as big as it feels from outside it.
My colleague does a language exchange twice a week and never stops.
A language exchange works until one of you is more polite than the other.
So what do I do differently?
Put in the hours at a fixed time, ten minutes, before you decide anything. Immersion helps too, and it can start with your phone's language.
I can keep it up for two weeks. Week three is where I quietly disappear.
Then plan week three today. Put something easy in it and let yourself enjoy it.
And if it gets dull?
Stick with it for three weeks. Dull is what it feels like right before it works.

title: The last flat bit
setting: Three months in, everything has stopped feeling better.

lines.t: I've stopped improving. Same work, no difference.
You've hit a plateau. It's the most normal thing in this room.
In the first three months I came on in leaps and bounds. Now nothing.
Leaps and bounds is the beginner's discount. It runs out around month four for everybody.
It doesn't feel normal. It feels like the ceiling.
It's the last flat bit before you start to think in English. Most people quit four weeks before it ends.
How would I even know it's ending?
Stop counting words. Count the calls you didn't dread.
That's fewer than it was, actually.
There's your measurement. The breakthrough arrives on an ordinary Tuesday, in a sentence you didn't plan.
My sister picked up Italian in a year, apparently.
Children pick up a language. Adults learn one and then say they picked it up.
I did dream in English last week. Once.
Then tell somebody. That one's real, and the phrase you fought with in March is second nature by now.
